newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Egypt, Jordan blame Netanyahu for peace crisis.
newsitem.headline: Egypt, Jordan blame Netanyahu for peace crisis.

text.p: The only two Arab states at peace with Israel blamed Prime Minster Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday for a breakdown in peacemaking which has spawned waves violence in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

In the volatile West Bank town of Hebron, Israeli soldiers shot and wounded at least 24 Palestinians on Friday while fighting protesters who hurled fire bombs and stones, witnesses said. Two Israeli border policemen were lightly wounded.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said his country's bid to break the four-month-old impasse, triggered by Israeli settlement building, failed due to Netanyahu's obstinance.

"There has been no progress and the Israeli government has not budged from its position...The responsibility for the tension rests with Israel," Moussa said in an interview published on Friday in the Israeli daily Haaretz newspaper.

Egyptian envoy Osama el-Baz has shuttled between Israel and the PLO searching for a formula to revive peace talks which Palestinians say can only resume when the Jewish state halts construction at a settlement site in Arab East Jerusalem.
Netanyahu has ruled out a building freeze.
Jordan's King Hussein, Netanyahu's closest Arab ally, said he was "despairing more and more" over Palestinian-Israeli peace talks and expressed disappointment in Israel.

"Prime Minister Netanyahu is a person who will be judged in time...I gave him all the support I could initially -- he was the choice of the Israeli people for the post of prime minister of Israel," Hussein told the British Broadcasting Corporation in an interview.

"But I must admit I am very disappointed in the performance as a whole of Israel and of its government and its leadership in the present and the recent past. I really hope we will see some improvement before it is too late," he said.
Egypt was the first Arab country to make peace with Israel, signing a accord in 1979. Jordan and Israel reached an peace agreement in 1994.
Netanyahu was elected more than a year ago promising "peace with security" and a tougher line in negotiations with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Peacemaking with the PLO since then has lurched from crisis to crisis.

The latest violence erupted two weeks ago in Hebron -- where 400 Jewish settlers live among 100,000 Palestinians -- when a right-wing Jewish woman put up posters ago depicting the Moslem Prophet Mohammad as a pig.

Witnesses said masked Arabs flung scores of petrol bombs and some home-made explosive charges at Israeli soldiers who fired live ammunition and rubber-coated metal bullets from rooftops and from behind barricades along Shallaleh street, which divides Hebron into Israeli and PLO-controlled sections.

Medics at a Palestinian field clinic set up behind the line of clashes said they evacuated at least 24 people wounded by live ammunition or knocked down by the rubber bullets. Two teenagers were in serious condition after being hit in the head.
